description: Wang's static-take family film and the representation of diasporic Chinese-American grief.
content_html:
Production Context: Lulu Wang’s The Farewell (2019)

The Farewell was directed and written by Lulu Wang, expanding on her 2016 This American Life episode ‘In Defense of Ignorance’ — her own family’s experience of the Chinese cultural practice of withholding a terminal diagnosis from a dying relative. The film was produced by Big Beach, Depth of Field, Kindred Spirit and Ray Productions, and distributed by A24 in the United States and Entertainment One internationally. Cinematographer Anna Franquesa Solano shot the film; the score was composed by Alex Weston, used sparingly. Editors Matthew Friedman and Michael Taylor cut the film. Made for around $3 million, the film was shot largely in Changchun, China, with some New York sequences. It premiered at Sundance 2019 and won the Independent Spirit Award for Best Feature; Awkwafina won the Golden Globe for Best Actress in a Musical or Comedy, the first actress of Asian descent to win in that category.

Key Fact

The Farewell (2019) was directed by Lulu Wang and shot by Anna Franquesa Solano in Changchun, China. Awkwafina stars as Billi; the score is by Alex Weston. The film was distributed by A24 and premiered at Sundance 2019. Awkwafina won the Golden Globe for Best Actress — the first actress of Asian descent to win in that category.

Representation Focus: Diasporic Chinese-American Identity and Grief

The written-paper question on global non-English-language film focuses on representation. In The Farewell, the central representational concern is the diasporic Chinese-American experience: the particular position of people who inhabit two cultural frameworks simultaneously and whose grief, communication and moral values do not map cleanly onto either. Billi, the New York-based protagonist, returns to China for a wedding that is itself a socially organised deception — the family has agreed not to tell the grandmother, Nai Nai, that she has terminal cancer, following a Chinese cultural norm. Billi’s objection to this practice is partly American, partly personal, and partly generational: the film represents the hyphenated identity not as a problem to be resolved but as a permanent condition to be inhabited.

Wang’s representational strategy relies on formal restraint: long static takes, wide ensemble framing during family meals, a score used sparingly, and language-shift cuts between Mandarin and English. These micro choices collectively construct a film in which grief is expressed through indirection and cultural ritual, not through dramatic declaration — a representational argument that the emotional register of the hyphenated experience does not translate into Hollywood convention.

Micro Analysis: The Opening Billi-and-Nai-Nai Phone Call

The film opens with a split-screen telephone conversation between Billi in New York and Nai Nai in China. Wang and Solano use a medium close-up for Billi — framed against the cold light and neutral walls of a New York interior — and a slightly warmer, softer framing for Nai Nai, set within the familiar domestic clutter of the Changchun apartment. The micro contrast between these two lighting and spatial registers is immediate: even in the same phone call, the two characters inhabit visually different worlds. At the macro level, this opening sequence represents the diasporic condition at the most fundamental level: physical separation, connected by a communication technology that simultaneously shows proximity and distance. The warmth of Nai Nai’s space codes China as the emotional centre of the film, even as Billi’s New York frame is her current reality.

One of The Farewell’s most analytically productive micro features is the language-shift cut: scenes begin in Mandarin and switch to English, or cut between the two languages mid-sequence, without the conventional transition devices — no subtitle change, no visual shift — that non-English-language cinema typically employs to signal a language change. The cut is on the language itself. At the macro level, these cuts represent the diasporic experience from the inside: for Billi, Mandarin and English are not two separate modes but the same continuous self expressed through two cultural registers. The language-shift cut refuses to position the spectator as an English-speaking outsider for whom Chinese needs translating; it positions the spectator within the bilingual world itself. This is a representational choice about whose perspective the film privileges.

Micro Analysis: The Wedding-Banquet Hall Set Piece

The wedding-banquet hall set piece is the film’s most formally complex sequence in terms of ensemble staging. Anna Franquesa Solano uses wide ensemble framing throughout: the large family group is held together in single frames rather than being broken into individual close-ups, and the long long takes hold the scene of social performance and suppressed grief in a single continuous observation. The lighting is warm and high-key — the festive surface of the occasion — but the static camera position means the spectator can watch the competing emotional registers of each character simultaneously: Nai Nai’s genuine pleasure, Billi’s contained anguish, the rest of the family maintaining the collective lie.

At the macro level, the ensemble framing in this sequence represents the family as a collective body engaged in a collective act of care — the withheld diagnosis. The mise-en-scène of the banquet — the round tables, the formal clothing, the abundance of food — codes this as a Chinese cultural ritual in which social performance and emotional suppression are not hypocrisy but a form of love. This is the film’s central representational argument about the diasporic cultural ethics: the withheld diagnosis is an act of tenderness, not deception.

Key Fact

The Farewell’s key sequences for micro/representation analysis are: (1) the opening Billi-and-Nai-Nai phone call; (2) the airport-arrival and family-greeting sequence; (3) the wedding-banquet hall set piece; (4) the hospital scan-results sequence; (5) the closing slow-motion street-walk. These five sequences build the film’s sustained representational argument about diasporic grief, cultural translation and the expressiveness of formal restraint.

Micro Analysis: The Closing Slow-Motion Street-Walk

The closing sequence of The Farewell uses a single sustained slow-motion family walk through the streets of Changchun. Solano holds the wide frame, and the slow motion extends the duration of a gesture — the family together in a public street — that would otherwise be entirely ordinary. The non-diegetic score (Alex Weston) enters here for one of its rare appearances, gentle and unhurried, coding the sequence as elegiac rather than triumphant. The slow motion does not aestheticise the family as a spectacle; it gives the ordinary act of walking together an emotional weight that the rest of the film’s formal restraint has been building toward.

At the macro level, the closing sequence represents the diasporic condition at its most tender: the family together in China, which may be one of the last times, and the spectator understanding through the slow-motion frame that what they are watching is already passing. The film’s representational argument about grief is made not through dialogue or dramatic declaration but through a formal choice — slowing time — that embeds the emotional reality in the visual texture of the image.

Students sometimes approach representation questions by asking whether a film is an ‘accurate’ or ‘fair’ portrait of the group it depicts. This is not the analytical question. Representation in film studies asks how a group is constructed for the spectator through specific filmic choices — regardless of whether those choices map onto any individual’s lived experience. In The Farewell, the relevant question is not ‘does this film accurately represent Chinese culture?’ but ‘which specific camera position, lighting state, editing decision or sound choice in the wedding-banquet set piece constructs the withheld diagnosis as an act of collective care rather than individual dishonesty, and what does that construction argue about how the diasporic family is represented for the spectator?’
exam_tip_html: In representation questions on The Farewell, the most common error is to focus on the cultural theme (the withheld diagnosis, Chinese family values) without connecting those themes to the film’s specific micro choices. The long takes, the sparse score, the language-shift cuts, the warm-versus-cool lighting contrast between New York and Changchun — these are the analytical levers. Every paragraph must name a sequence, identify a specific micro choice, and explain what representational argument that choice makes. For extended-essay questions, aim to argue a thesis about how the film represents diasporic identity as a condition of cultural translation rather than cultural loss, and use at least two named sequences to support that argument.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Farewell (2019), directed by Lulu Wang and shot by Anna Franquesa Solano, uses long static takes, wide ensemble framing, a sparse score and language-shift cuts to represent the diasporic Chinese-American experience as one of grief expressed through cultural indirection rather than dramatic declaration.
  • The contrast between warm Changchun interiors and cold New York framing is established from the opening phone-call sequence and sustained throughout, representing the emotional geography of the diasporic protagonist.
  • Effective representation answers name specific sequences, specify micro choices (long take, wide ensemble frame, slow motion, language-shift cut), and explain the representational argument each makes about diasporic identity, grief and cultural ethics.

practice_questions.text: Identify the production company that distributed The Farewell (2019) in the United States.
Define the term 'long take' and explain why it is a significant formal choice in The Farewell.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly defining a long take as an extended uncut shot that holds a scene in continuous observation without conventional editing interruption; 1 mark for explaining its significance in The Farewell specifically (e.g. the long takes in ensemble scenes allow the spectator to observe the competing emotional registers of all family members simultaneously within a single unbroken frame, representing the family's collective suppression of grief).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the contrast in lighting and spatial framing between the Billi sequences in New York and the Nai Nai sequences in Changchun in the opening phone-call sequence of The Farewell represents the diasporic condition. What effect does this contrast produce for the spectator?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying the lighting contrast (cold light and neutral walls in New York; warmer, softer framing for Nai Nai in Changchun); 1 mark for linking this to the opening phone-call sequence specifically; 1 mark for explaining the representational argument (even in the same phone call, the two characters inhabit visually different worlds; China is coded as the emotional centre); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the spectator (physical separation and proximity are simultaneously present; the diasporic condition is visualised as a split between two worlds); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (e.g. medium close-up, mise-en-scène, diasporic identity, cinematography, representation).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how cinematography and mise-en-scène work together in the wedding-banquet hall set piece of The Farewell to represent the family's collective act of grief and care. Stay inside this sequence and refer to at least three distinct micro features.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response stays inside the wedding-banquet sequence and unpacks at least three distinct micro features (e.g. wide ensemble framing holding the whole family simultaneously in a single frame, long takes allowing competing emotional registers to coexist without editorial interruption, warm high-key banquet lighting that codes the festive surface, the mise-en-scène of round tables and formal clothing as Chinese cultural ritual). Each micro feature is linked to the representational argument that the withheld diagnosis is a collective act of care rather than individual deception. Specialist vocabulary precise throughout.
Secure: At least two micro features with explanation of representational effect; argument present though one feature may be less fully developed.
Developing: Relevant features mentioned but generic; effect on spectator implied not stated.
Emerging: Plot description; no named sequence; minimal specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Lulu Wang uses cinematography and sound in The Farewell to represent diasporic Chinese-American identity. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach an evaluative judgement about the film's representational choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained thesis on how the film represents diasporic identity as a condition of cultural translation and grief expressed through indirection. At least two named sequences analysed in depth with concrete micro features (e.g. the lighting contrast and medium close-up framing in the opening phone-call sequence; the wide ensemble framing and long takes in the wedding-banquet set piece; the slow motion and sparse score in the closing street-walk; the language-shift cuts as a representational device throughout). Micro choices are linked to macro representational arguments about diasporic identity, collective grief and cultural ethics. AO1 context (Wang's autobiographical source, the Sundance premiere, the A24 distribution, the cultural practice of withheld diagnosis) is integrated to support AO2 analysis. A justified evaluative judgement on the effectiveness of the film's representational project closes the essay. Specialist vocabulary precise and consistent.
Secure: At least two named sequences with generally concrete micro analysis; representational argument present; evaluative judgement attempted.
Developing: Relevant points but thin micro analysis; plot description dominates some paragraphs; evaluative judgement absent or vague.
Emerging: Plot retelling; no thesis; minimal specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how the opening phone-call sequence and the closing slow-motion street-walk use cinematography and sound to represent Billi's relationship to her diasporic identity at different points in the film. Match one specific micro choice from each sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An explicit comparative line runs through the response — matching the cold medium close-up framing and split-world contrast of the opening phone call (the diasporic condition as physical separation and emotional longing) against the slow motion and gentle score of the closing street-walk (the same condition as something elegiac and temporally extended, the ordinariness of being together given extraordinary weight). The response explains what each micro choice constructs representationally and accounts for the narrative shift across the film (arrival of information vs departure from a world that may be ending). A synthesised judgement on what the contrast between these two registers says about the film's overall representational arc closes the response. Specialist vocabulary precise.
Secure: Both sequences referenced with at least one specific micro choice each; comparative link present; contextual judgement attempted.
Developing: Both sequences mentioned separately; micro features are vague; no explicit comparative line.
Emerging: Only one sequence discussed; no comparative structure.

knowledge_checks.q: What cultural practice is at the centre of The Farewell's narrative?
options: An arranged marriage between Billi and a Chinese student
The family withholding a terminal diagnosis from the grandmother
Billi returning to China to compete in a national film competition
The family staging a protest at a hospital

knowledge_checks.q: What does 'diasporic identity' mean in the context of The Farewell?
options: The experience of people who live in a small rural community
The experience of people living outside their ancestral homeland, navigating two cultural frameworks
The identity of a film director who works across multiple countries
A term for the emotional impact of watching a foreign-language film

knowledge_checks.q: The Farewell (2019) was shot largely in _____, China, by cinematographer Anna Franquesa Solano.
In The Farewell, the language-shift cuts between Mandarin and English represent the diasporic experience as one of _____, not translation between two separate identities.
options: two cultural frameworks as part of the same continuous self

knowledge_checks.q: Match each sequence from The Farewell to its representational function:
right: Lighting contrast between New York and Changchun represents the diasporic split between two worlds
Wide ensemble framing and long takes represent the family's collective act of love expressed as shared deception
Slow motion and sparse score give the ordinary act of walking together the weight of an impending farewell

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the cinematographer on The Farewell?
Which distributor released The Farewell in the United States?
What award did Awkwafina win for The Farewell?
flashcard_questions.a: Golden Globe for Best Actress — the first actress of Asian descent to win in that category.
The experience of people living outside their ancestral homeland, navigating two cultural frameworks.
An extended uncut shot that holds a scene in continuous observation without editorial interruption.

flashcard_questions.q: What is slow motion in film?
flashcard_questions.a: A technique where increased frame rate during shooting makes playback appear slowed, extending a moment emotionally.
How people, groups or ideas are constructed for the spectator through filmic choices.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the warm Changchun lighting versus cold New York framing represent from the opening phone-call sequence?
flashcard_questions.a: China as the emotional centre; New York as Billi's current but less warm reality — the diasporic split.
Everything placed within the frame: set, costume, lighting, props, blocking, performance.

flashcard_questions.q: In the wedding-banquet set piece, what representational argument do the wide ensemble frames and long takes make?
flashcard_questions.a: The family's collective lie is a collective act of love — grief expressed through shared social performance.

flashcard_questions.q: The Farewell is based on what personal source material by Lulu Wang?
flashcard_questions.a: Her 2016 This American Life episode 'In Defense of Ignorance' about her own family.

glossary_terms.definition: The way in which people, groups, places or ideas are constructed and presented to the spectator through filmic choices.
The experience and self-understanding of people living outside their ancestral homeland, often navigating between two cultural frameworks simultaneously.
An extended uncut shot that holds a scene in a single continuous take, avoiding the fragmentation of conventional editing.
A shot that holds a group of characters together in the frame simultaneously, typically using a medium-wide or wide-angle composition.
A cinematographic effect in which the frame rate is increased during shooting so that playback appears slowed, typically used to extend a moment emotionally or aesthetically.
A shot that frames the subject from approximately the chest upward, balancing intimacy with spatial context.
Everything placed within the camera's field of view to create meaning, including set design, costume, lighting, props, blocking and performance.
